entries.title: A button teaches twice
entries.event_semantics: Portal's 2007 release anchors the production study. Swift's 2009 recollections and the 2008 Swift/Wolpaw interview are later accounts, not contemporary student-project documentation.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Kim Swift remembers Narbacular Drop beginning with a practical question: how could the team use portals that David Kircher had been experimenting with? Swift, Jeep Barnett and Garret Rickey had already made student projects together at DigiPen. Their environmental puzzle emerged from several proposals, rather than a complete vision delivered by one designer. In her later account, presenting it at Valve led to an offer to rebuild the idea using Source. The familiar hiring story also contains years of classmates learning to work together.

One Portal room was meant to teach players to carry a box onto a button. Swift recalls that people instead stood on the button themselves, opening a distant door, then fired a portal through it. The team inserted glass so this room would teach the intended action. Elsewhere, they deliberately used the solution those players had discovered. An apparent mistake had produced two useful outcomes: a clearer lesson in one chamber, and an additional possibility to develop in another part of the game.

After a playtest, writer Erik Wolpaw asked players to recount the story. When several people missed something, he took that as a reason to reconsider the presentation. Sometimes the team removed information; sometimes it moved a detail into the environment. Swift describes watching expressions as well as actions. A player who solved a room might still be bored or confused about its meaning. Observing both responses gave the writing and level design a shared problem to work on while there was time to change it.

GLaDOS also developed through repeated recording sessions with Ellen McLain. Wolpaw describes writing towards the actor's strengths as the project continued, rather than treating her contribution as a single final delivery. Her performance helped the team make a machine sound increasingly human as the player's actions undermined it. Swift and Wolpaw's discussion keeps several kinds of authorship in view: puzzles, dialogue, performance and the people testing them. A room could change what the voice needed to say, and the voice could change how that room felt.

entries.title: Making a script fit
entries.event_semantics: The 1994 English Final Fantasy VI / North American Final Fantasy III production is the anchor. A September 1994 interview discusses several projects; a February 2007 retrospective supplies the specific Final Fantasy III workflow. Secret of Mana's deadline is not silently assigned to Final Fantasy VI.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: In a 1994 interview, Ted Woolsey describes translating text that had to fit inside an existing game. Enlarging dialogue windows helped only so far. Shortening a sentence could disturb information needed later in the plot, while messages arrived without a convenient reading order. His example is Secret of Mana, whose scattered text made following the story difficult. The work required remembering connections that the translation files did not display together. A clear English line still had to function at its particular place in the program.

Woolsey also discussed selecting games for American and European release. He expected to visit Square in Japan and examine projects in development, describing a growing role for the overseas office. These were choices about audiences and production as well as vocabulary. The interview mentions plans for Final Fantasy V that should be read as plans at that moment, not a record of a completed release. Preserving that distinction lets the interview show what a localization worker could anticipate before later decisions changed the published history.

Looking back in 2007, Woolsey described the Super Nintendo game Americans knew as Final Fantasy III: the Japanese Final Fantasy VI. He received a cartridge, files and some unfinished strategy-guide material. The text was divided among many separate files rather than arranged as a continuous script. He had asked for a complete set of videotapes but said it never arrived. That specific recollection matters beside his earlier account of usual working methods: the resources available on one project were not a fixed procedure across every game.

His first English delivery was too large, and another shortening pass still failed to fit. Woolsey recalls finally reworking individual sections while preserving their information and the timing of scripted actions. A small team in Japan adjusted memory allocation and other parts of the localized version. Only after the text fitted could he see a playable build containing it. These constraints help explain why translation decisions leave visible traces in a game. They do not settle whether every alteration was necessary or every resulting line successful.

entries.title: The people behind the bracket
entries.event_semantics: Battle by the Bay in 1996 anchors this selected history of tournament organisation. Evo's institutional retrospective and an organiser's account of the 2016 event are distinct, later perspectives; this is not a complete survey of fighting-game communities.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Evo's own history begins in Northern California. In 1996, Tony Cannon and Tom Cannon worked with online Street Fighter communities to gather players at Sunnyvale Golfland for Battle by the Bay. Super Street Fighter II Turbo and Street Fighter Alpha 2 supplied two different contests. The account remembers Alex Valle defeating John Choi in the Alpha 2 final. Before the event could have a famous result, somebody had to connect the people discussing these games with a place where they could actually meet and play.

The same institutional history follows later meetings to Folsom and, in 2002, to UCLA under the Evolution name. Its account of the 2001 tournament includes Japanese competitors alongside American players, with different games producing different champions. Those details resist treating a community as one permanent group or one style of play. Organisers were maintaining a meeting across changing software, venues and participants. The name became more recognisable, while the practical work still depended on arranging particular matches between people who had travelled to be there.

Andrés Velasco y Coll describes another route into that work. He hosted tournaments at Florida International University, later met Evo organiser Albert Carmona, and offered technical help at Carmona's home arcade. Judging pools and updating brackets followed. Looking back on Evo 2016, he explains that his responsibilities included assembling a team, training judges, making schedules and handling disputes. This was work participants might notice mainly when it failed. A competitive match needed people to know where to go, whose turn came next and which rules applied.

That interview also records shortcomings rather than an uninterrupted success story. Velasco y Coll discusses delayed Mortal Kombat X semifinals and accepts responsibility for insufficient planning. He describes paper brackets whose updates could overwhelm the staff processing them, and argues for digital tools. These are an organiser's explanations, not an independent evaluation of every disputed match. They nevertheless make the scale problem concrete: adding competitors does not simply produce more excitement. It also increases the information, equipment and time that somebody must coordinate fairly.

entries.title: Who gets to rate a game?
entries.event_semantics: The 9 December 1993 US Senate hearing anchors this institutional case, followed through the March 1994 hearing and ESRB's later chronology. Witness concerns are not presented as scientific findings about media effects; this is a US system, not worldwide law.
entries.summary: From a hearing to a label.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: On 9 December 1993, senators Joseph Lieberman and Herb Kohl held a joint hearing about violent video games and information for parents. The Senate committee's later report records testimony from educators and other witnesses, as well as representatives including Nintendo's Howard Lincoln and Sega's Bill White. It says industry representatives committed to creating a rating system for the 1994 holidays. The document preserves its concerns and commitments. It does not, by recording them, establish that the witnesses' claims about violence were proven.

A second joint hearing on 4 March 1994 examined the industry's preliminary proposal. According to the committee report, a central question was how the system could demonstrate independence and credibility. Retail representatives also supported participating in a future scheme. The practical issue extended beyond deciding which words belonged on a box: publishers and shops would have to recognise the same process. This record helps distinguish a proposal discussed under political pressure from a government agency directly classifying every game offered for sale in the United States.

The ESRB's own chronology dates its foundation to 1994, under the Interactive Digital Software Association. It records five rating categories and seventeen content descriptors at the system's announcement. These were two different kinds of information: an age category and details about the material inside. The organisation's account is useful for following its published structure, while remaining its own institutional history. It should not stand in for evidence that every parent interpreted a label alike, or that the system resolved every disagreement over a game's content.

The labels and their administration changed after that first announcement. ESRB records an advertising code in 1995, the replacement of Kids to Adults with Everyone in 1998, and an Advertising Review Council in 2000. Its chronology also places a sanctions system in 2000, including points, fines and corrective action. Rating a product and policing how companies market it had become related responsibilities. Looking at the dates separately prevents the familiar present-day symbols from being projected backwards as though the whole scheme had arrived fully formed.

entries.title: A puzzle crosses the border
entries.event_semantics: The 1989 licensing negotiations anchor the feature. Pajitnov's 1989/1993 interviews and Rogers' 2023 account are participant perspectives, not court findings. The 1984/1985 creation-date discrepancy is not resolved here; the feature does not use the film as factual evidence.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: In a 1993 interview, Alexey Pajitnov recalled making games alongside his work at the Soviet Academy of Sciences' computer centre. Tetris, he said, spread abroad through word of mouth and unauthorised copies. He connected its appeal to rhythm, randomness and decisions made in real time, while remaining cautious about psychological explanations of its success. The creator's account moves between the work of programming and the experience of watching a program escape its original setting. Its international audience did not begin as one orderly, centrally managed launch.

Pajitnov's 1989 comments describe a different problem: what a licence actually permitted. In discussing the Nintendo and Tengen dispute, he distinguished personal-computer rights from home-console rights and objected to treating them as interchangeable. This is his account of a contested chain of permissions, not a substitute for the contracts or a judicial decision. It explains why the hardware category mattered to participants. The same falling blocks could appear on several machines while the authority to sell each version remained a separate question to negotiate.

Henk Rogers later recalled carrying a Japanese console version into ELORG's Moscow offices and discovering that its rights were disputed. In Jack Yarwood's interview, Rogers describes having cartridges in manufacture and family property committed as collateral. He was also pursuing handheld rights after arguing that Nintendo should include Tetris with Game Boy in North America. These are a business participant's recollections of his own exposure. They show why a conversation about apparently simple software could involve manufacturing commitments, different licence categories and considerable personal pressure.

Interviewed about the 2023 Tetris film, Rogers praised its ability to communicate a complicated negotiation while acknowledging compression and invention. He described watching an extended part of his life accelerated into a feature film. That distinction matters when photographs, interviews and screen drama sit together in a museum. A participant's approval does not turn every filmed incident into a documented event. The film offers its own characterisation and pace; the interviews preserve qualifications, conflicting expectations and negotiations that do not fit so neatly into a chase.

entries.title: Building somewhere to explore
entries.event_semantics: Myst's 1993 release anchors two separate retrospective interviews with Robyn Miller in November and December 2012. Recollections of prototypes and changing plans are not an exact dated production diary. No claim that Myst or The Manhole was the first CD-ROM game.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: When Robyn Miller recalled Myst's origins, the commission mattered alongside the brothers' ideas. Cyan made children's software, but Sunsoft wanted something for an older audience. The opportunity gave Rand and Robyn room to develop another kind of world. Robyn also names collaborators: Chuck Carter contributed art, Chris Brandkamp sound, and Richard Watson HyperCard scripting. Listing those jobs changes the familiar image of two brothers making an island alone. The finished environment depended on several people turning a proposal into pictures, behaviour and sound.

Robyn describes taking inspiration for the interface from ordinary objects: doors, switches and other things a visitor already knows how to use. He imagined a novice, including his grandmother, rather than assuming familiarity with a game controller. This was a design ambition, not proof that nobody would become confused. The same interview describes ideas being rejected when a better one appeared. Myst's apparent solidity therefore hides revisions. Familiar actions could make an unfamiliar place approachable, but the team still had to decide which actions belonged there.

In a separate interview, Robyn recalls an early planning period spent drawing maps, devices and puzzles, then explaining the world aloud to collaborators. He likens it to tabletop role-playing: describing arrival at the dock and asking what someone would do next. Plans involved collecting keys before the designers settled on pages. The scene was being tested as a sequence of expectations before every view existed. A drawing could expose a missing connection, and another person's question could send the imagined walk in a different direction.

Robyn remembered composing by looking at a particular area of the game and waiting for an idea to emerge. He identifies the Proteus MPS+ as the limited synthesizer setup used for sounds, effects and mixing. Chris Brandkamp's sound work also belongs in that account. Music itself had not been guaranteed: Robyn says a version without it preceded the publisher's request to try adding it. The resulting score was a production decision made against the pictures, rather than an inevitable accompaniment specified before the world took shape.

entries.title: Choosing where to look
entries.event_semantics: Super Mario 64's 1996 release anchors the first half; a 2013 Nintendo developer conversation supplies a later, deliberately different camera solution. The later multiplayer design is not attributed to the 1996 game, and no universal invention claim is made.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Shigeru Miyamoto described a difficult change during Super Mario 64's development. Earlier games let designers measure a jump in pixels. In three dimensions, players struggled to judge distance, so the team adjusted the levels to accept jumps that were sufficiently close. He remembered making that change when development was already far along. More dimensions did not simply mean more precise simulation. The view through which players judged an action changed what the game could reasonably demand, and the designers altered the rules around that practical limit.

The development interviews also describe a prototype with Mario and Luigi moving around a room, using the analogue stick and changing the camera at a button press. Moving the character was meant to be enjoyable before courses and enemies supplied further goals. Programmers and designers then discussed terrain, depth calculations and what could appear in front of what. These were connected tasks rather than separate finishing touches. A useful camera required a world it could describe clearly, while the world had to accommodate a moving character and viewpoint.

In Nintendo's 2013 conversation about Super Mario 3D World, Yoshiaki Koizumi described a different starting point. The team had experience with a camera that maintained a set distance and direction, reducing the need to rotate around a course. Multiplayer narrowed the options further. They rejected split-screen and worked towards a shared view that could hold the players together. This was a response to that game's particular format, not a declaration that free cameras were obsolete. Deciding who must remain visible was part of designing the activity itself.

The discussion preserves another option. Kenta Motokura points out that single players could use a free-camera mode driven by the Wii U GamePad's gyro sensor. Koizumi describes it as a way for experienced players to seek immersion. Iwata distinguishes this extra control from what someone must master to finish a course. Camera operation could therefore be an optional layer rather than a constant admission test. Across these accounts, the useful question is specific: which decisions should this player need to make, in this room, with these controls?

entries.title: A city in a small file
entries.event_semantics: The 2017 release of Ctrl-Alt-Test's H–Immersion anchors one concrete demoscene production. The Finnish community's heritage account supplies wider practice, not proof that this modern Windows intro ran on a Commodore 64. National inventory documentation is not a claim of UNESCO World Heritage designation.
entries.summary: Immersion makes its materials with code.
entries.editorial_credit: Original English feature written for Pixel Museum; primary creators, interviewers, translators and institutions credited per card.
body: Ctrl-Alt-Test's Windows PC intro Immersion depicts a city rising from the sea, rendered as a non-interactive presentation in real time. The work belongs to the 64k intro category: its program, rather than a stored movie, must fit into a very small executable. Algorithms generate the materials needed for its pictures and sound. The distinction matters when a museum shows a video capture. That recording communicates the composition, but it is evidence of one run of software whose construction is itself part of the creative work.

The group traces its idea to a conversation after watching competitors at Revision 2015. They hoped to return with something comparable, missed the following year's deadline, and released a version in 2017. Their postmortem acknowledges that the second half was unfinished. Work continued before the final version appeared that December. The story concerns tools and taste as well as file size: an image of a submerged city gave the team something to build towards, while a competition deadline exposed the distance between that intention and its implementation.

The Finnish demoscene's living-heritage submission describes people collaborating on code, graphics and music, then showing the results at parties. Competitions make those roles visible to an audience, often through public voting. It names Assembly, which began as a demo party in Helsinki in 1992, alongside smaller gatherings. These occasions help explain why making the executable is only part of the activity. A work also needs an opportunity to run, other people to watch it, and a community able to discuss what it is doing.

That community account also follows changing methods of exchange: floppy disks, modem connections and later internet distribution. It identifies preservation as work the scene has largely carried out for itself while museums take increasing interest. Keeping a file is one task; keeping knowledge of its tools and presentation is another. The account is a submission by participating communities, not a neutral census of everyone involved. Read that way, it documents how practitioners describe the things they want to transmit, including skills, gatherings and relationships around the finished productions.
